This results in significant property damage, supply chain disruptions, property price declines, declining insurance affordability and an economic decline in QLD. Long-term drought impacting the agriculture portfolio Assumes a severe drought across large areas of Australia lasting for 10 years. There is a simultaneous rise in interest rates due to unrelated economic factors, stable commodity prices globally and declines in farm property values in the high drought impacted areas. Extended electricity outage in New South Wales Assumes two ageing coal-fired power stations in NSW become inoperable for up to six months. This results in rolling blackouts which impact productivity of high energy usage industries. 152 CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Why we ran this scenario Droughts have been a feature of the Australian landscape throughout history and can have severe impacts on the environment, industries, economy and people. Climate change is increasing temperatures and affecting rainfall, evaporation and climate systems in Australia, with climate projections indicating that droughts may be more severe and last longer. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank should a long-term drought lead to a substantial decline in farm values. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes a severe drought lasting for 10 years across parts of the Murray-Darling Basin and Western Australia. The scenario assumes farm values decline in the high-drought impact areas, the drought occurs during a high interest rate environment for reasons unrelated to the drought and the effectiveness of government support declines over the scenario. Insights from our analysis Total losses to the Bank over the 10 years are assessed to be below $500 million, split relatively evenly between farming – mainly grain growing, mixed farming and beef cattle farming – and agriculture adjacent industries, mainly from food manufacturing and farm produce wholesaling. The maximum loss in any individual year under this scenario does not exceed $100 million. Why we ran this scenario AEMO noted in the 2024 ISP that 90% of Australia’s coal- fired power generators are forecast to retire by 2035, and are becoming less reliable and more difficult to maintain. Investment is needed urgently and new generation, storage and firming must be in place before coal-fired power stations retire. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank from a long-term electricity outage caused by two coal-fired power stations becoming simultaneously inoperable. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes two ageing NSW coal-fired power stations, responsible for approximately 40% of NSW electricity supply, become simultaneously inoperable for six months, leading to energy price increases and rolling blackouts. Wholesale electricity prices are assumed to increase fourfold, with retail prices increasing from year two by 30%. Electricity supply is assumed to be prioritised for residential and commercial businesses, however high energy consuming businesses, particularly in manufacturing, are required to reduce production. The scope of this exercise was limited to manufacturing industries and the economic impacts on retail customers. This is based on the assumption that electricity would be prioritised to other high electricity usage sectors such as retail, commercial and services, electricity, gas, water and waste services. Insights from our analysis This combination of increased wholesale electricity prices and reduced production leads to estimated credit losses to the Bank from the manufacturing sector of below $200 million over five years. The greatest losses arise from the manufacturing sub-industries of transport equipment, machinery and equipment, food and chemical manufacturing. Energy price increases of 30% in retail do not drive material retail credit losses for the Bank, with losses estimated to be below $100 million driven by a slight economic downturn. Climate change is increasing temperatures and affecting rainfall, evaporation and climate systems in Australia, with climate projections indicating that droughts may be more severe and last longer. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank should a long-term drought lead to a substantial decline in farm values. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes a severe drought lasting for 10 years across parts of the Murray-Darling Basin and Western Australia. The scenario assumes farm values decline in the high-drought impact areas, the drought occurs during a high interest rate environment for reasons unrelated to the drought and the effectiveness of government support declines over the scenario. Insights from our analysis Total losses to the Bank over the 10 years are assessed to be below $500 million, split relatively evenly between farming – mainly grain growing, mixed farming and beef cattle farming – and agriculture adjacent industries, mainly from food manufacturing and farm produce wholesaling. The maximum loss in any individual year under this scenario does not exceed $100 million. Why we ran this scenario AEMO noted in the 2024 ISP that 90% of Australia’s coal- fired power generators are forecast to retire by 2035, and are becoming less reliable and more difficult to maintain. Investment is needed urgently and new generation, storage and firming must be in place before coal-fired power stations retire. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank from a long-term electricity outage caused by two coal-fired power stations becoming simultaneously inoperable. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes two ageing NSW coal-fired power stations, responsible for approximately 40% of NSW electricity supply, become simultaneously inoperable for six months, leading to energy price increases and rolling blackouts. Wholesale electricity prices are assumed to increase fourfold, with retail prices increasing from year two by 30%. Electricity supply is assumed to be prioritised for residential and commercial businesses, however high energy consuming businesses, particularly in manufacturing, are required to reduce production. The scope of this exercise was limited to manufacturing industries and the economic impacts on retail customers. This is based on the assumption that electricity would be prioritised to other high electricity usage sectors such as retail, commercial and services, electricity, gas, water and waste services. Insights from our analysis This combination of increased wholesale electricity prices and reduced production leads to estimated credit losses to the Bank from the manufacturing sector of below $200 million over five years. The greatest losses arise from the manufacturing sub-industries of transport equipment, machinery and equipment, food and chemical manufacturing. Energy price increases of 30% in retail do not drive material retail credit losses for the Bank, with losses estimated to be below $100 million driven by a slight economic downturn.
